chapters.title: Chapter 5: GST Basics for Business Owners

lessons.title: GST Registration, Returns and the Compliance Mistakes That Cost Money

body.text: Income tax forgives a slow month. GST does not. It runs on a monthly clock, the penalties are arithmetic rather than judgement, and a business that falls three months behind starts losing customers, because its buyers cannot claim credit for invoices it has not reported.

children.text: The previous lesson covered how GST works. This one covers what it asks of you: when you must register, what you file and by when, and the specific failures that turn a manageable tax into a cash problem.

body.text: Aggregate turnover is computed across all your GST registrations on the same PAN, across every state, and includes exempt supplies and exports, not just taxable sales. Owners routinely measure one state or one product line, conclude they are below the limit, and discover otherwise during an audit.

columns.label: Reasons to register voluntarily
points: You can claim input tax credit on your own purchases
Business customers prefer suppliers who let them claim credit
You can supply inter-state and sell through e-commerce platforms
Tenders and larger buyers usually require a GSTIN

columns.label: Reasons to wait
points: Monthly returns start immediately, whether or not you have sales
Your prices rise for customers who cannot claim credit, such as individuals
Late fees apply even to nil returns
Cancelling later is a process, not a switch

body.title: The composition scheme, for very small businesses

children.text: Small businesses can opt to pay a flat percentage of turnover instead of running the full credit mechanism. Broadly, traders and manufacturers pay 1%, restaurants 5%, and other service providers 6% under a separate scheme, with turnover limits of ₹1.5 crore for goods and ₹50 lakh for services. Check the current limits for your state before opting in.

The trade-offs are severe and often missed. You cannot claim input tax credit on your purchases, you cannot charge GST to your customers, so they get no credit either, you cannot make inter-state supplies, and you issue a bill of supply rather than a tax invoice. That makes the scheme sensible for a business selling directly to consumers, and usually wrong for one selling to other businesses.

body.text: GSTR-1 is the one that affects other people. Your customers' credit comes from what you file there, so a late GSTR-1 is not just your problem, it is your customer's working capital sitting blocked. Large buyers track this, and some hold payments until the credit appears in their GSTR-2B.

body.title: Try It: The Cost of Paying Late
body.prompt: A business owes ₹6,00,000 of GST for a month and pays it 45 days after the due date. At 18% a year, what interest does it owe? Answer in rupees.
body.explanation: ₹6,00,000 × 18% × 45 ÷ 365 comes to about ₹13,315. Interest runs per day, not per month, which is the opposite of the income tax rules you met in Chapter 4, where a part of a month counts as a whole month. Note also that it is 18% on late tax but 24% where credit was wrongly claimed and used.

body.text: An invoice that should have been an e-invoice but was not is treated as no invoice at all. That means your customer cannot claim the credit, and the supply is treated as unreported. Businesses crossing ₹5 crore for the first time need to switch their billing system before the new year starts, not after the first customer complains.

body.title: Quick Check: Who Must Register?
body.question: Four small businesses are all below ₹20 lakh of turnover. Which one must still register for GST?
options: A bakery in Nagpur selling only to walk-in customers in Maharashtra
A Surat trader who ships fabric to buyers in Rajasthan and Delhi
A freelance designer with three clients in her own city
A tuition centre providing exempt educational services locally
body.explanation: Making inter-state supplies of goods requires registration regardless of turnover, so the Surat trader must register from the first consignment. The bakery and the designer are below the thresholds and supplying within their own state. Exempt services do not create a registration liability on their own, though aggregate turnover still includes exempt supplies when you test the threshold for anything else.

children.text: The Five Mistakes That Actually Cost Money

body.caption: Common failures and what they do to you

cells: Filing GSTR-3B without reconciling GSTR-2B
Credit claimed that the portal does not support, recoverable later with interest at 24%
Charging CGST and SGST on an inter-state supply
Customer loses the credit, you pay the right tax again, and reclaim the wrong one through a refund process
Treating blocked credits as claimable
Reversal with interest, and a recurring audit finding since the same category repeats every month
Missing returns for several periods
Late fees stack up, filing gets blocked because returns must go in sequence, and registration can eventually be cancelled
Ignoring the reverse charge on notified purchases
Tax payable in cash with interest, even though the credit may have been available if you had paid on time

body.title: Scenario: Composition Looked Cheaper
body.scenario: A Ludhiana trader supplies auto parts, almost entirely to garages and workshops that are themselves GST registered. Turnover is about ₹90 lakh a year. His consultant suggests the composition scheme, pointing out that 1% of turnover is only ₹90,000 a year and the paperwork is much lighter than monthly returns.
body.prompt: Is the composition scheme right for this business?
body.modelAnswer: Almost certainly not, and the reason has nothing to do with the ₹90,000. Under composition, he cannot charge GST on his invoices, which sounds attractive until you see it from the buyer's side: his garage customers get no input tax credit from him, while a regular competitor's invoice gives them full credit. For a business customer, a supplier whose tax cannot be recovered is effectively 18% more expensive, so he either loses the customer or absorbs the difference in his price. He also cannot claim credit on his own purchases, so the GST on the parts he buys becomes a real cost rather than a pass-through, and 1% of turnover sits on top of that. And because composition suppliers cannot make inter-state supplies, he would be locked out of buyers in neighbouring states, which for an auto parts trader in Ludhiana is a serious constraint. The scheme is designed for businesses selling to final consumers, such as a neighbourhood restaurant or a retail shop, where no one is asking for credit. A business-to-business trader at ₹90 lakh should stay in the regular scheme, and can use the QRMP option to file quarterly while paying monthly, which addresses the paperwork concern without any of these costs.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Return That Settles the Money
body.textWithBlank: The monthly summary return through which output tax, input credit and the net payment are declared is ___, generally due on the 20th of the following month.
body.explanation: GSTR-3B. GSTR-1 reports your sales invoice by invoice and feeds your customers' credit, while GSTR-3B is where the tax is actually computed and paid. Both matter, but they fail in different ways: a late GSTR-1 hurts your customers, and a late GSTR-3B costs you interest.

body.label: Non-filing is not a quiet failure
body.context: You cannot skip a period and file the next one. Missed months block later filings, fees accumulate on each, and sustained non-filing can lead to cancellation of registration, which stops you issuing valid tax invoices at all.

body.title: A GST Month That Runs Itself
steps: Raise every sales invoice with the correct GSTIN, place of supply and tax split, and e-invoice it if you are above the threshold
Reconcile GSTR-2B against the purchase ledger before claiming any credit in GSTR-3B
File GSTR-1 by the 11th so your customers' credit is not held up
Pay and file GSTR-3B by the 20th, even in a month with no sales
Keep a running list of invoices unpaid beyond 150 days, ahead of the 180-day reversal
Reconcile GST turnover with the turnover in your books every quarter, not at year end
Diarise the annual return and reconciliation statement by 31 December
Review your aggregate turnover against the e-invoicing and QRMP thresholds at the start of each year

cards.definition: All supplies on one PAN across every state, including exempt supplies and exports, used to test registration and scheme thresholds.
The state-wise registration number issued under GST, based on your PAN.
The return reporting outward supplies invoice by invoice, which feeds your customers' GSTR-2B.
The monthly summary return where output tax and credit are declared and the net tax is paid.
Quarterly returns with monthly payment, available to taxpayers with turnover up to ₹5 crore.
A flat percentage of turnover for small businesses, with no input credit, no tax charged to customers and no inter-state supply.
An invoice reported to the government portal before issue, mandatory above the prescribed turnover for business-to-business supplies.

points: Registration is compulsory above ₹40 lakh for goods and ₹20 lakh for services, with lower limits in specified states
Some situations require registration regardless of turnover, including inter-state supplies of goods, e-commerce selling and reverse charge liability
Aggregate turnover covers every registration on your PAN and includes exempt supplies and exports
GSTR-1 by the 11th feeds your customers' credit, and GSTR-3B by the 20th settles your own tax
Interest runs at 18% a year on late tax and 24% where credit was wrongly availed and used, calculated per day
The composition scheme suits businesses selling to consumers and usually hurts those selling to other businesses
E-invoicing applies above ₹5 crore, and an invoice that should have been e-invoiced is treated as no invoice at all
Returns must be filed in sequence, so skipped months block later filings and can end in cancellation

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax advice. GST thresholds, due dates, scheme limits, late fee caps and e-invoicing requirements are set through notifications and GST Council decisions and change frequently, and several differ by state. Verify the current figures on the GST portal or with a qualified GST practitioner before acting on them.
